parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin -archa, from Latin -archēs, from Ancient Greek -άρχης (-árkhēs), from ἀρχή (arkhḗ, “rule”, “government”).
Inherited from Old Spanish -izar, a learned borrowing from Late Latin -izāre. Doublet of -ear, which was inherited.
Borrowed from Late Latin -mantia, from Ancient Greek μαντεία (manteía, “divination”).
Borrowed from Late Latin acolythus, from Ancient Greek ἀκόλουθος (akólouthos).

parole.significato: aphorism (short phrase conveying some principle or concept of thought)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin aphorismus, from Ancient Greek ἀφορισμός (aphorismós).
Borrowed from Late Latin anachoreta, from Ancient Greek ἀναχωρητής (anakhōrētḗs).
Borrowed from Late Latin Anacreonticus, from Ancient Greek Ἀνακρέων (Anakréōn), Anacreon a Greek poet.
Borrowed from Late Latin anagramma, from Ancient Greek ἀνά (aná, “up, back”) + γράμμα (grámma, “letter”).
Borrowed from Late Latin anathema, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἀνάθεμα (anáthema, “something dedicated, especially dedicated to eternal damnation”), from ἀνᾰτίθημῐ (anătíthēmĭ) + -μᾰ (-mă).
Borrowed from Late Latin anatomicus, from Ancient Greek ἀνατομικός (anatomikós), from ἀνατομή (anatomḗ, “a cutting up”). See anatomía.
Borrowed from Late Latin antiphrasis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίφρασις (antíphrasis).
Borrowed from Late Latin antithesis, from Ancient Greek ἀντίθεσις (antíthesis), from ἀντί (antí, “against”) + θέσις (thésis, “position, stance”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin anōnymus.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin apocalypsis, from Ancient Greek ᾰ̓ποκᾰ́λῠψις (ăpokắlŭpsis, “revelation”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apologēticus, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογητικός (apologētikós).

Borrowed from Late Latin apologia, from Ancient Greek ἀπολογία (apología, “a speech in defence”), from ἀπόλογος (apólogos, “an account, story”), from ἀπό (apó, “from, off”) + λόγος (lógos, “speech”). In the “expression of remorse” sense, a calque of English apology, and most common in Llanito, consi
Borrowed from Late Latin poplexia or Latin apoplexia, from Ancient Greek ἀποπληξίᾱ (apoplēxíā), from ἀποπλήσσω (apoplḗssō) to cripple by a stroke; ἀπο- (apo-, “from”) + πλήσσω (plḗssō, “to strike”).

parole.significato: apocope (loss or omission of a sound or syllable from the end of a word)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin apocŏpe, from Ancient Greek ἀποκοπή (apokopḗ), ἀποκόπτω (apokóptō, “cut off”).

Borrowed from Late Latin apocryphus (“secret, not approved for public reading”), from Ancient Greek ἀπόκρυφος (apókruphos, “hidden, obscure”), thus "(books) of unknown authorship", from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + κρύπτω (krúptō, “to hide”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostata, from Ancient Greek ἀποστάτης (apostátēs).

Borrowed from Late Latin apostolus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστολος (apóstolos, “messenger, one sent forth”), from ἀποστέλλω (apostéllō, “to send off”), from ἀπό (apó, “from”) + στέλλω (stéllō, “to set”).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostrŏphe, from Ancient Greek ἀποστροφή (apostrophḗ).
Borrowed from Late Latin apostrŏphus, from Ancient Greek ἀπόστροφος (apóstrophos).

Inherited from Old Spanish arcidiano, arçidiano, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archidiaconus, based on Ancient Greek ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + διάκονος (diákonos, “servant, minister”). Doublet of archidiácono.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin archīvum, from Ancient Greek ἀρχεῖον (arkheîon).
Borrowed from Late Latin archangelus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχάγγελος (arkhángelos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἄγγελος (ángelos, “messenger, angel”).
Borrowed from Late Latin arōma (“spices”), from Ancient Greek ἄρωμα (árōma, “seasoning, spicy and/or fragrant smell”).
Equivalent to artro- + -itis, from Late Latin arthrītis, from Ancient Greek ἀρθρῖτις (arthrîtis), from ἄρθρον (árthron, “joint”).
From Old Spanish arçobispo, from Late Latin archiepiscopus, from Ancient Greek ἀρχιεπίσκοπος (arkhiepískopos), from ἀρχι- (arkhi-, “chief”) + ἐπίσκοπος (epískopos, “overseer”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ascēta, from Ancient Greek ἀσκητής (askētḗs).
From Late Latin asphaltum, from Ancient Greek ἄσφαλτος (ásphaltos, “asphalt, bitumen”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin asteriscus, from Ancient Greek ἀστερίσκος (asterískos, “a little star, asterisk”), diminutive of ἀστήρ (astḗr, “star”), used in manuscripts to mark passages.
Borrowed from Late Latin astrologicus, from Ancient Greek ἀστρολογικός (astrologikós). By surface analysis, astrología + -ico.
Borrowed from Late Latin barytŏnus, from Ancient Greek βαρύτονος (barútonos).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin biōticus. By surface analysis, bio- + -t- + -ico.
Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmia, from Ancient Greek βλασφημία (blasphēmía, “slander, blasphemy”).
Borrowed from Late Latin blasphēmus, from Ancient Greek βλάσφημος (blásphēmos).

parole.significato: any member of the species Leporinus obtusidens of ray-finned fish (characin)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin bōca, from Ancient Greek βῶκα (bôka), accusative of βῶξ (bôx), a contracted form of βόαξ (bóax), from βοῦς (boûs, “ox”) + ὤψ (ṓps, “eye”).
Inherited from Late Latin bursa. Doublet of bursa. Cognate with English burse (“purse”).

parole.significato: wineskin, bota bag; soft pouch, usually suspended from a cord or lanyard, for carrying wine or other beverages (similar…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin buttis, with a change of suffix, and probably of Ancient Greek origin. Compare English butt (“large cask”).
Borrowed from Late Latin bufalus, from Latin būbalus, from Ancient Greek βούβαλος (boúbalos, “antelope, wild ox”).
Ultimately from Ancient Greek καῦμα (kaûma), through Late Latin cauma. Possibly through the intermediate of Italian calma, although the word was found in Ibero-Romance as early as in Italian.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin camomilla, from Latin chamaemēlon, borrowed from Ancient Greek χᾰμαίμηλον (khămaímēlon).

Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin canonicus (“canon”), from Ancient Greek κανονικός (kanonikós). Cognate with Portuguese cónego, Galician cóengo. The sense of “corn salad” seems to come by ellipsis from (hierba de los) canónigos.

parole.significato: face (the front part of the head)
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin or Vulgar Latin cara, from Ancient Greek κάρα (kára, “head, face”).
Borrowed from Late Latin charisma, from Ancient Greek χάρισμα (khárisma, “favorable disposition; grace, favor”), from χάρις (kháris, “favor, grace”), from χαίρω (khaírō, “to be happy”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catacumbae, dissimilation of Latin cata- (“among”) (from Ancient Greek κατά (katá, “under”)) + tumbas.
Borrowed from Late Latin catarrhus, from Ancient Greek κατάρροος (katárrhoos, “catarrh, head cold”), from καταρρέω (katarrhéō, “to flow down”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin catēchūmenus, from Ancient Greek κατηχούμενος (katēkhoúmenos, “being instructed”), present participle passive of κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to sound through, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).
Borrowed from Late Latin, Ecclesiastical Latin cathedrālis, from cathedra, from Ancient Greek καθέδρᾱ (kathédrā, “seat”). Equivalent to cátedra + -al.
Borrowed from Late Latin catēgoria, from Ancient Greek κατηγορία (katēgoría).
Borrowed from Late Latin catēchēsis, from Ancient Greek κατήχησις (katḗkhēsis, “oral instruction”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to instruct orally”).
Borrowed from Late Latin catēchista, from Ancient Greek κατηχιστής (katēkhistḗs, “oral instructor”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to instruct orally”).

Borrowed from Late Latin catēchizāre (“to teach by word of mouth”), from Ancient Greek κατηχίζω (katēkhízō, “to instruct orally”), from κατηχέω (katēkhéō, “to resound, instruct orally”), from κατά (katá, “down”) + ἠχή (ēkhḗ, “sound, noise”).
From Late Latin catheterismus, from Ancient Greek καθετηρισμός (kathetērismós).

parole.significato: catheter (a small tube inserted into a body cavity)
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Late Latin catheter, from Ancient Greek καθετήρ (kathetḗr).
Borrowed from Late Latin catholicus, from Ancient Greek καθολικός (katholikós, “universal”), from κατά (katá, “according to”) + ὅλος (hólos, “whole”).
Borrowed from Late Latin cephalaea, from Ancient Greek κεφαλαία (kephalaía), from κεφαλή (kephalḗ, “head”).
Inherited from Late Latin zelōsus, from zelus, from Ancient Greek ζῆλος (zêlos, “zeal, jealousy”). Compare Italian geloso, French jaloux.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin coemētērium, from Ancient Greek κοιμητήριον (koimētḗrion, “sleeping chamber”). Probably influenced by Spanish cemento, whence the intrusive n.

Inherited from Old Spanish ceresa, from Late Latin ceresia, from the neuter plural of ceresium, assimilated form of Latin cerasium, borrowed from Ancient Greek κερᾰ́σῐον (kerắsĭon, “cherry (fruit)”), from κερᾰσός (kerăsós) + -ῐον (-ĭon). Cognate with English cherry, Galician cereixa, Portuguese cere
Borrowed from Late Latin cyclus (“cycle”), from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”). Doublet of chakra.
Borrowed from Late Latin sciaticus, variant of ischiadicus, from Ancient Greek ἰσχιαδικός (iskhiadikós), the adjective of ἰσχίον (iskhíon, “hip”).
Borrowed from Late Latin clīma (“climate”), from Ancient Greek κλῐ́μᾰ (klĭ́mă, “region, zone”), from κλῐ́νω (klĭ́nō, “to slope, to incline”).
Inherited from Old Spanish clerigo, a semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin clēricus, from Ancient Greek κληρικός (klērikós).

parole.significato: copper (reddish-brown, malleable, ductile metallic element with high electrical and thermal conductivity, symbol Cu, an…
parole.testo: Inherited from Late Latin cuprum (“copper”), from Latin cyprium (aes) (“Cypriot copper”), from Ancient Greek Κύπρος (Kúpros), because Cyprus was its chief source. The irregular evolution of this term in Spanish and other Ibero-Romance languages like Portuguese cobre (with the expected result being *
Borrowed from Late Latin chrisma, from Ancient Greek χρῖσμα (khrîsma, “anointing”), from χρίω (khríō, “to anoint”), from Proto-Indo-European *gʰrēy- (“to smear”).
Inherited from Old Spanish cannamo, from Late Latin cannabum, from Latin cannabis, from Ancient Greek κάνναβις (kánnabis, “hemp”). Doublet of cannabis.
Borrowed from Late Latin daemōniacus, from Ancient Greek δαιμονιακός (daimoniakós).
From Late Latin diaphorēticus, from Ancient Greek διαφορητικός (diaphorētikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoea, from Ancient Greek διάρροια (diárrhoia, “through-flowing”), from διά (diá, “through”) + ῥέω (rhéō, “to flow”).
Borrowed from Late Latin diarrhoicus, from Ancient Greek διαρροϊκός (diarrhoïkós), from διάρροια (diárrhoia). Assimilated to diarrea.
Borrowed from Late Latin diphthongus, itself borrowed from Ancient Greek δίφθογγος (díphthongos).
Borrowed from Late Latin diūrēticus, from Ancient Greek διουρητικός (diourētikós), from διουρέω (diouréō, “to pass urine, have diuretic properties”).

parole.significato: diocese (administrative district in some ancient Roman provinces)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin diocēsis, from Latin dioecēsis, from Ancient Greek διοίκησις (dioíkēsis, “administration; diocese”).
Borrowed from Late Latin doga (“vessel”), from Ancient Greek δοχή (dokhḗ, “receptacle”). Doublet of duela.
Borrowed from Late Latin dogmatizāre, from Ancient Greek δογματίζω (dogmatízō, “to opine, to decree”), from δόγμα (dógma, “opinion, tenet”).
Borrowed from Late Latin dogmaticus, from Ancient Greek δογματικός (dogmatikós).

Learned borrowing from Late Latin dosis, from Ancient Greek δόσις (dósis, “a portion prescribed”, literally “a giving”), from Proto-Hellenic *dótis, from Proto-Indo-European *déh₃tis. Doublet of dote.
From Late Latin ecclēsiasticus (“of the church”), from Ancient Greek ἐκκλησιαστικός (ekklēsiastikós), from ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía).
Borrowed from Late Latin oecūmenicus, from Ancient Greek οἰκουμενικός (oikoumenikós).
From Late Latin encliticus, from Ancient Greek ἐγκλιτικός (enklitikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin encōmium, from Ancient Greek ἐγκώμιον (enkṓmion), neuter form of ἐγκώμιος (enkṓmios), from ἐν (en, “in”) + κῶμος (kômos, “festival, revel”).
Borrowed from Late Latin entelechīa, from Ancient Greek ἐντελέχεια (entelékheia).

Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasmus, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιασμός (enthousiasmós, “inspiration, enthusiasm”), from ἔνθεος (éntheos, “possessed by a god”), from ἐν (en, “in”) + θεός (theós, “god”).
Borrowed from Late Latin enthūsiasta, from Ancient Greek ἐνθουσιαστής (enthousiastḗs, “inspired”). See entusiasmo.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin epicy̆clus, from Ancient Greek ἐπίκυκλος (epíkuklos). By surface analysis, epi- + ciclo.
Borrowed from Late Latin epiphanīa, from Ancient Greek ἐπιφάνεια (epipháneia), from ἐπί (epí, “upon”) + φαίνω (phaínō, “to shine, appear”).
Borrowed from Late Latin epiglottis.
Borrowed from Late Latin epilēpsia, from Ancient Greek ἐπιληψία (epilēpsía).
Borrowed from Late Latin epistola, from Ancient Greek ἐπιστολή (epistolḗ).
Borrowed from Ecclesiastical Latin Late Latin erēmīta, from Ancient Greek ἐρημίτης (erēmítēs).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin scandalizō, from Ancient Greek σκανδαλίζω (skandalízō). By surface analysis, escándalo + -izar.

Borrowed from Late Latin scarificāre, from Latin scarifāre (“to scarify”), from Ancient Greek σκαριφᾶσθαι (skariphâsthai, “scratch”), from σκάριφος (skáriphos, “writing, drawing, sketching”). Equivalent to escarbar (“to dig”) + -ificar.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin sphēra, from Latin sphaera, borrowed from Ancient Greek σφαῖρᾰ (sphaîră, “ball, globe”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin sphincter, from Ancient Greek σφιγκτήρ (sphinktḗr, “band, contractile muscle”), from σφίγγω (sphíngō, “to bind tight”).
Borrowed from Late Latin spermatĭcus, from Ancient Greek σπερματικός (spermatikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin eucharistia, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστία (eukharistía, “thanksgiving”).

parole.significato: eucharistic (of or relating to the Eucharist)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin eucharisticus, from Ancient Greek εὐχαριστικός (eukharistikós). By surface analysis, eucaristía + -ico.
Borrowed from Late Latin euphōnia, from Ancient Greek εὐφωνία (euphōnía, “sweetness of voice”), from εὖ (eû, “well”) + φωνή (phōnḗ, “sound, voice”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ēvangelizāre, from Ancient Greek.
Borrowed from Late Latin exorcizāre, from Ancient Greek ἐξορκίζω (exorkízō), from ἐξ (ex) + ὅρκος (hórkos, “oath”).
Borrowed from Late Latin phallus, from Ancient Greek φαλλός (phallós).
From Old Spanish pharaon, from Late Latin Pharaōnem, from Ancient Greek φαραώ (pharaṓ), from Hebrew פַּרְעֹה (par‘ōh), from Egyptian pr-ꜥꜣ (“great house”), pr:aA
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phaenomenon, from Ancient Greek φαινόμενον (phainómenon, “thing appearing to view”).
Borrowed from Late Latin physiologicus, from Ancient Greek φυσιολογικός (phusiologikós).
From Late Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (phusiognōmía), from φυσιογνωμονία (phusiognōmonía).
From Late Latin physiognomia, from Ancient Greek φυσιογνωμία (phusiognōmía), from φυσιογνωμονία (phusiognōmonía).
From older flegma, borrowed from Late Latin phlegma, from Ancient Greek φλέγμα (phlégma, “flame, inflammation, phlegm”), from φλέγω (phlégō, “to set on fire, to burn”).
Borrowed from Late Latin phlegmāticus, from Ancient Greek φλεγματικός (phlegmatikós). By surface analysis, flema + -ático.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin phrasis (“diction”), from Ancient Greek φράσις (phrásis, “manner of expression”).
Borrowed from Late Latin geneālogia, from Ancient Greek γενεαλογία (genealogía), from γενεά (geneá, “generation, descent”) and -λογία (-logía, “study of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin glōssa, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă).

parole.significato: tap, faucet (device used to dispense liquids)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish grifo, a learned borrowing from Late Latin grȳphus (“griffin”), from Latin grȳps, borrowed from Ancient Greek γρῡ́ψ (grū́ps). Noun sense 1 (“faucet”) comes from the ornamentations which fountain faucets commonly bore, which often featured griffin heads. Compare Aragonese j
Borrowed from Late Latin hēmistichium, from Ancient Greek ἡμιστίχιον (hēmistíkhion).
Borrowed from Late Latin heptagōnus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἑπτάγωνος (heptágōnos), from ἑπτά (heptá, “seven”) + γωνίᾱ (gōníā, “corner, angle”) + -ος (-os).

Borrowed from Late Latin heteroclitus, from Ancient Greek ἑτερόκλιτος (heteróklitos), from ἕτερος (héteros, “other, another, different”) + κλίνω (klínō, “lean, incline”), the latter from Proto-Indo-European *ḱley-.
From Late Latin hydromantia, from Ancient Greek ὑδρομαντεία (hudromanteía); corresponding to hidro- + -mancia.
Inherited from Old Spanish ydropisia, from Late Latin hydropisia, from Latin hydropisis, from Ancient Greek ὕδρωψ (húdrōps, “edema”), from ὕδωρ (húdōr, “water”). Compare with English dropsy.
Borrowed from Late Latin hypnōticus, from Ancient Greek ὑπνωτικός (hupnōtikós, “inducing sleep, soporific”).

Borrowed from Late Latin hippocampus (“sea horse”), from Ancient Greek ἱππόκαμπος (hippókampos, “sea horse, hippocamp”, from ἵππος (híppos, “horse”) + κάμπος (kámpos, “sea monster”)), describing a mythological creature with a horse's forepart and a fishlike hindquarter.

Borrowed from Late Latin hypocrisis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόκρισις (hupókrisis, “answer, stage acting, pretense”), from ῠ̔ποκρῑ́νομαι (hŭpokrī́nomai, “to reply”), from ὑπό (hupó, “under, hypo-”) + the middle voice of κρῑ́νω (krī́nō, “to separate, to judge, to decide”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin hippopotamus, from Ancient Greek ἱπποπόταμος (hippopótamos, “river horse”).
Borrowed from Late Latin hypothesis, from Ancient Greek ὑπόθεσις (hupóthesis, “base, basis of an argument”).
Borrowed from Late Latin holocaustum, from Ancient Greek ὁλόκαυστος (holókaustos).

Inherited from an ellipsis of Late Latin pariēs fōrmācea (“a moulded wall”), from fōrmāceus, in reference to its being made by stuffing between two boards. Related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Reflects pared's change of gender from the original masculine. Compare hormazo and hor
Inherited from Late Latin fōrmācium, substantivised from fōrmāceus (“made in a mould”), related to Ancient Greek μορφή (morphḗ, “a shape, form”). Compare hormaza and horma (“dry stone wall”).
Inherited from Late Latin orphanus, from Ancient Greek ὀρφανός (orphanós, “without parents, fatherless”).  PIE word  *h₃órbʰos
Borrowed from Late Latin idioma, from Ancient Greek ἰδίωμα (idíōma, “peculiarity; idiom”).
Borrowed from Late Latin īrōnicus, from Ancient Greek εἰρωνικός (eirōnikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin iūdaismus, from Ancient Greek Ἰουδαϊσμός (Ioudaïsmós, “Judaism”), from Hebrew יְהוּדָה (Yehuda, “Judah”).
From Late Latin lecanomantia, from Ancient Greek λεκανομαντείᾱ (lekanomanteíā, “lekanomanteía”), from λεκάνη (lekánē, “dish, pan”) + -mancia.
Borrowed from Late Latin leopardus, from Ancient Greek λεόπαρδος (leópardos), from λέων (léōn, “lion”) + πάρδος (párdos, “male panther”), a later form of πάρδαλις (párdalis, “leopard”).
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin litanīa, from Ancient Greek λιτανεία (litaneía, “prayer”), from λιτή (litḗ, “supplication”).
Borrowed from Late Latin levisticum, probably an alteration of Latin ligusticum, from Ligusticus (“Ligurian”), ultimately from Ancient Greek Λίγυς (Lígus).
Borrowed from Late Latin lītūrgia, from Ancient Greek λειτουργία (leitourgía).
Borrowed from Late Latin logicus.
Borrowed from Late Latin magīa, from Ancient Greek μαγεία (mageía).
Borrowed from Late Latin manna, from Ancient Greek μάννα (mánna), from Hebrew מָן (mān).
Borrowed from Late Latin maniacus, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μανιακός (maniakós), adjectival form of μανία (manía, “madness”). See manía.

Inherited from Late Latin māchināre (“mill, grind”), a verb based on Latin māchina (“device, mill”), an early borrowing from Ancient Greek. Compare Italian macinare. Morphological doublet of maquinar, a borrowing from Latin.
Borrowed from Late Latin melancholia, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολία (melankholía, “blackness of the bile”).
Borrowed from Late Latin melancholicus, from Ancient Greek μελαγχολικός (melankholikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin metempsychōsis, itself a borrowing from Ancient Greek μετεμψύχωσις (metempsúkhōsis).
Borrowed from Late Latin metōnymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).
Borrowed from Late Latin metathesis, from Ancient Greek μετάθεσις (metáthesis), from μετά (metá, “among”) + θέσις (thésis, “placement”).
Borrowed from Late Latin mȳriadem, from Ancient Greek μῡριάδος (mūriádos, “number of 10,000”), from μῡρῐ́ος (mūrĭ́os, “numberless, countless, infinite”, literally “10,000”).
From Late Latin mȳthologia, borrowed from Ancient Greek μῡθολογῐ́ᾱ (mūthologĭ́ā).
Borrowed from Late Latin monarcha, from Ancient Greek μονάρχης (monárkhēs), variant of μόναρχος (mónarkhos, “sole ruler”).
Borrowed from Late Latin monarchia, from Ancient Greek μοναρχία (monarkhía).

parole.significato: monogamy (a permanent pair bond between two beings)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin monogamia, from Ancient Greek μονογαμία (monogamía), equivalent to mono- + -gamia.
Borrowed from Late Latin monasticus.
Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthicus, from Ancient Greek μῡθικός (mūthikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin necromantīa, from Ancient Greek νεκρομαντεία (nekromanteía), from νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) + μαντεία (manteía, “divination”); corresponding to necro- + -mancia.
From Late Latin necrōsis, from Ancient Greek νέκρωσις (nékrōsis).
Borrowed from Late Latin nephrītis, from Ancient Greek νεφρῖτις (nephrîtis).
Borrowed from Late Latin nosocomīum, from Ancient Greek νοσοκομεῖον (nosokomeîon, “hospital”), from νόσος (nósos, “disease, illness”) + κομέω (koméō, “to take care of”).
Borrowed from Late Latin Oasis (“name of various oases”), from Ancient Greek Ὄασις (Óasis), from Demotic Egyptian wḥj, from Egyptian wḥꜣt (“oasis, cauldron”), G43-V28-G1-X1:N25.
Borrowed from Late Latin ochra, from Ancient Greek ὠχρός (ōkhrós, “yellow”) (modern Greek ωχρός (ochrós)).
Borrowed from Late Latin oligarcha, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγάρχης (oligárkhēs).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin oligarchicus, from Ancient Greek ὀλιγαρχικός (oligarkhikós). By surface analysis, oligarquia (“oligarchy”) + -ico (“-ic”, adjective-forming suffix).
Borrowed from Late Latin onomatopoeïa, from Ancient Greek ὀνοματοποιία (onomatopoiía). More at onomatopoeia.
Learned borrowing from Late Latin orthodoxia, from Ancient Greek ὀρθοδοξία (orthodoxía, “right opinion”). By surface analysis, ortodoxo + -ia.
Borrowed from Late Latin orthodoxus, from Ancient Greek ὀρθόδοξος (orthódoxos, “having the right opinion”).
Borrowed from Late Latin ōidium, from Ancient Greek ὠΐδιον (ōḯdion), diminutive of ᾠόν (ōión, “egg”).

Inherited from Old Spanish parabla by metathesis, from Late Latin, from Latin parabola (“comparison; later, speech”), from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ, “comparison; parable”). Doublet of parábola, a borrowing. Compare English parley, palaver, parable and parole.
Borrowed from Late Latin paradīgma, from Ancient Greek παράδειγμα (parádeigma).
Borrowed from Late Latin paragōgē, from Ancient Greek παραγωγή (paragōgḗ, “derivation, addition”).
Borrowed from Late Latin parallēlogrammum, from Ancient Greek παραλληλόγραμμον (parallēlógrammon, “bounded by parallel lines”), from παράλληλος (parállēlos, “parallel”) + γραμμή (grammḗ, “line”).
Borrowed from Late Latin parochia, alteration of Ancient Greek παροικία (paroikía, “dwelling abroad”), from παρά (pará, “beside”) + οἶκος (oîkos, “house, dwelling”).
Learned borrowing from Late Latin parabola, from Ancient Greek παραβολή (parabolḗ). Doublet of palabra. The mathematical sense is taken from New Latin or directly from Greek.
Borrowed from Late Latin parenthesis (“addition of a letter to a syllable in a word”), from Ancient Greek παρένθεσις (parénthesis).
From Late Latin pasmus, from Ancient Greek σπασμός (spasmós, “spasm”). Doublet of espasmo.
Borrowed from Late Latin pentagōnum, from Ancient Greek πεντάγωνον (pentágōnon, “pentagon”), neuter form of πεντάγωνος (pentágōnos, “five-angled”). Equivalent to penta- + -gono.

parole.significato: parchment (material, made from a polished animal skin, used like paper for writing)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish pergamino, from Late Latin *pergamīnus. Compare Portuguese pergaminho.

Borrowed from Late Latin peripherīa, from Ancient Greek περιφέρεια (periphéreia, “circumference, outer surface”), from περιφερής (peripherḗs, “moving around, circular, round”), from περιφέρω (periphérō, “to carry around”), from περί (perí, “around”) + φέρω (phérō, “to bear, carry”).
Borrowed from Late Latin peritonaeum, from Ancient Greek περιτόναιον (peritónaion).
From Late Latin pyromantīa, from Ancient Greek πυρομαντεία (puromanteía), from Ancient Greek πῦρ (pûr), πῠρός (pŭrós). Equivalent to piro- + -mancia.
Borrowed from Late Latin pityriāsis, from Ancient Greek πιτυρίασις (pituríasis), from πίτυρον (píturon, “bran”).

parole.significato: Pythia (priestess presiding over the Oracle of Apollo at Delphi)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin pȳthōnissa, from Ancient Greek Πυθία (Puthía, “Pythia”).
Borrowed from Late Latin pleonasmus, from Ancient Greek πλεονασμός (pleonasmós), from πλεονάζω (pleonázō, “to be superfluous”).

From prática (archaic variant of práctica), by hypercorrection (replacing /ɾ/ with unetymological /l/ as a reverse-reaction to a medieval sound change that would replace /l/ with unetymological /ɾ/ after occlusive consonants), borrowed from Late Latin practica, from Ancient Greek πρακτική (praktikḗ,
Borrowed from Late Latin plēthōra (plētūra in Classical Latin), from Ancient Greek πληθώρη (plēthṓrē, “fullness”), from πλήθω (plḗthō, “to fill”).

parole.significato: polygamy (the condition of having more than one spouse)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin polygamia, from Ancient Greek πολυγαμία (polugamía), equivalent to poli- + -gamia.
Borrowed from Late Latin presbyterĭum.

parole.significato: prism (a polyhedron with parallel ends of the same size and shape)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin prisma, from Ancient Greek πρῖσμα (prîsma, literally “thing sawed”).
Borrowed from Late Latin problematicus, from Ancient Greek προβληματικός (problēmatikós), from πρόβλημα (próblēma, “outjutting, barrier, problem”).
Borrowed from Late Latin programma, from Ancient Greek πρόγραμμα (prógramma).

parole.significato: proselyte, convert (one who has recently converted to a religion or doctrine)
parole.testo: From Late Latin prosēlytus, from Ancient Greek προσήλυτος (prosḗlutos).
Borrowed from Late Latin prācticus.
Semi-learned borrowing from Late Latin paragraphus (early 15th century), from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos).
Borrowed from Late Latin pylōrus, from Ancient Greek πυλωρός (pulōrós, “gatekeeper”).
Inherited from Old Spanish cherubin, borrowed from Late Latin cherūbīm, plural of cherūb, from Ancient Greek χερούβ (kheroúb), from Hebrew כְּרוּב (kerúv).
Late Latin chȳlus, from Ancient Greek χυλός (khulós, “animal or plant juice”).

parole.significato: chyme (partly digested food passed from the stomach to the duodenum)
parole.testo: From Late Latin chymus, from Ancient Greek χυμός (khumós, “juice”).
Borrowed from Late Latin rabbi, from Ancient Greek ῥαββί (rhabbí, “rabbi”), from Hebrew רבי (rabbi, “my master”).
By metathesis from Late Latin liquirītia, from Ancient Greek γλυκύρριζα (glukúrrhiza, “sweet root”), influenced by liquor (“liquid”).
Borrowed from Late Latin rheuma.

parole.significato: rheumatic (relating to, suffering from or characterised by rheumatism)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin rheumaticus, from Ancient Greek ῥευματικός (rheumatikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin rhomboīdēs, from Ancient Greek ῥομβοειδής (rhomboeidḗs), from ῥόμβος (rhómbos, “rhombus”) + εἶδος (eîdos, “shape”).
Borrowed from Late Latin sabbaticus, from Ancient Greek σαββατικός (sabbatikós).
Inherited from Late Latin psalmus, from Ancient Greek ψαλμός (psalmós, “song sung to a harp, performance on a stringed instrument”), from ψάλλω (psállō, “to pluck an instrument”).
Borrowed from Late Latin psalmōdia, from Ancient Greek ψαλμῳδία (psalmōidía, “singing to a harp”), from ψαλμός (psalmós) + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, “song”).

Borrowed from Late Latin sarcasmus, from Ancient Greek σαρκασμός (sarkasmós, “sneer”), from σαρκάζειν (sarkázein, “to gnash the teeth”, literally “to tear off the skin”), based on σάρξ (sárx, “flesh”).
Borrowed from Late Latin synagōga, from Ancient Greek συναγωγή (sunagōgḗ, “assembly”).
From Late Latin synonymĭa, from Ancient Greek συνωνυμία (sunōnumía).
Borrowed from Late Latin synopsis, itself from Ancient Greek σύνοψις (súnopsis), from σύν (sún, “with or whole”) + ὄψις (ópsis, “view”) meaning “whole view”.

Borrowed from Late Latin syntaxis (“arrangement of words”), from Ancient Greek σύνταξις (súntaxis, “a putting together in order, arranging”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + τάξις (táxis, “arranging, arrangement”), from τάσσω (tássō, “to arrange”).

Borrowed from Late Latin synecdoche, from Ancient Greek συνεκδοχή (sunekdokhḗ, “jointly receiving”), from σύν (sún, “with”) + ἐκ (ek, “out of”) + δέχεσθαι (dékhesthai, “to accept”), this last element related to δοκέω (dokéō, “to think, suppose, seem”).
Borrowed from Late Latin Sirēna, from Sīrēn, borrowed from Ancient Greek Σειρήν (Seirḗn).
Borrowed from Late Latin systematicus, from Ancient Greek συστηματικός (sustēmatikós).
Borrowed from Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología), from ταὐτός (tautós, “identical”).

Borrowed from Late Latin theōria, from Ancient Greek θεωρία (theōría, “contemplation, speculation”), from θεωρός (theōrós, “spectator”), from θέα (théa, “a seeing, view”) + ὁράω (horáō, “to see, behold”).
From Late Latin tetrarcha, from Latin tetrarchēs, from Ancient Greek τετράρχης (tetrárkhēs). By surface analysis, tetra- + -arca.
From Late Latin theurgus, from Ancient Greek θεουργός (theourgós).
Borrowed from Late Latin tyrannizāre, borrowed from Ancient Greek τυραννίζω (turannízō). By surface analysis, tirano + -izar.

Inherited from Old Spanish tartuga, probably from the feminine of Late Latin tartarucchus or tartarūchus, a mythological spirit of Greek origin, from Ancient Greek ταρταροῦχος (tartaroûkhos), from Τάρταρος (Tártaros). Cf. also Medieval Latin tortūca.
Borrowed from Late Latin trapezium, from Ancient Greek τραπέζιον (trapézion).

Borrowed from Late Latin trophaeum, variant of Latin tropaeum (“trophy, victory memorial”), from Ancient Greek τρόπαιον (trópaion), from τροπή (tropḗ, “turning, trope”), from τρέπω (trépō, “to turn”).
Borrowed from Late Latin tropologicus, from Ancient Greek τροπολογικός (tropologikós).
Inherited from Late Latin trūcta, possibly from Ancient Greek τρώκτης (trṓktēs).
Borrowed from Late Latin tumba, from Ancient Greek τύμβος (túmbos).
Borrowed from Late Latin thymallus, from Ancient Greek θύμαλλος (thúmallos).

parole.significato: uncle (the brother, brother-in-law, or male cousin or cousin-in-law of either parent)
parole.testo: Inherited from Old Spanish tio, from Late Latin thius, from Ancient Greek θεῖος (theîos). Compare Italian zio, Galician tío and Portuguese tio, Sardinian tiu.
Inherited from Late Latin erĕmus, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἐρῆμος (erêmos), ἔρημος (érēmos, “lonely, solitary, desert, waste”).
Borrowed from Late Latin azȳmus, from Ancient Greek ἄζυμος (ázumos, “unleavened”), from ζύμη (zúmē, “leaven, sourdough”).
